evidence_passages: Weighted voting assigns a weight to each replica and requires that the sum of weights of participating replicas exceed a configured threshold; this allows the system to tolerate failures of many low-weight replicas provided the total remaining weight stays above the threshold.

reason: Available manufacturer and review sources show substantial variation depending on technology and build area: high‑end DLP/MSLA/LCD systems can reach pixel/voxel sizes below ~35 µm while many common desktop/mid‑range printers use ~50 µm; larger mid‑range or large‑format machines commonly have pixel sizes ≥100 µm. The proposition's bands (25–100 µm high‑end, 50–150 µm mid‑range) are broadly plausible but not a single standardized ‘typical’ across all vendors and form factors.

evidence_passages: “High-resolution 4K and 8K LCD screens achieve pixel sizes below 35 µm on compact printers, comparable to high-end DLP.”

Guides and comparisons of SLA/DLP/MSLA/LCD note that XY pixel/voxel size depends on projector/screen resolution and build area and ranges from a few tens of microns (high‑resolution machines) up to >100 µm for larger‑format systems.

reason: Manufacturer guides and peer‑reviewed literature show cure/penetration depth depends strongly on resin formulation and exposure; reported values span from a few tens of micrometres up to around 1 mm. The 0.2–1 mm window lies within reported ranges for many (especially clear/low‑pigment) resins but is not a universal ‘typical’ value for all resins (some commonly used pigmented or filled resins have much smaller cure depths).
queries: SLA DLP cure depth per exposure pass resin cure depth typical range manufacturer datasheet review paper
sources: Liqcreate – Resin 3D‑printing: Ec, Dp, cure depth & more explained (https://www.liqcreate.com/supportarticles/resin-cure-depth-ec-dp/)
Tailoring UV Penetration Depth in Photopolymerization (PMC/NIH) – review article (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11722631/)
Fundamentals of Stereolithography – 3DResyns (introductory guide)
evidence_passages: “The cure depth will always be finite, leading to a logarithmic correlation between the exposure and the cure depth… typical curves show sub‑millimetre cure depths that depend on resin formulation and exposure.”

“Penetration depths (Dp) and resulting cure depths depend on wavelength, absorber content and formulation; reported values in the literature range from a few tens of micrometres up to about one millimetre, depending on the resin.”
“Manufacturers specify cure depth / penetration as a resin‑dependent parameter and show that more highly pigmented or filled resins have much lower cure depths than clear formulations.”

reason: Multiple 3D‑printing design guides state the common “45° rule” (overhangs steeper than ~45° usually require supports) and note that support structures contact and mar the printed surface—i.e., they leave marks/scars on delicate lattice surfaces.
queries: overhang angle 45 degrees support lattice scar additive manufacturing 3D printing overhang guidelines
sources: 3D Printing Overhangs: Angles, Supports, and Materials — 3DMag (example discussion of the 45° rule) (https://www.3dmag.com/3d-wikipedia/3d-printing-overhang-support-angles-materials/)
The 45° rule in 3D printing — Sovol blog (discussion of using 45° to avoid supports) (https://sovol.eu/blogs/new/45-degree-rule-3d-printing-overhangs-support-quality-guide)
Prusa/Community guidance and forums — (practical user guidance that >45° often needs supports; removal can affect surface quality) (https://forum.prusa3d.com/)

3D Hubs / Hubs Knowledge Base — Design for 3D Printing: Overhangs & Supports (notes that supports are needed beyond ~45° and that support touchpoints affect surface finish) (https://www.3dhubs.com/knowledge-base/overhangs/)
evidence_passages: “The widely cited ‘45° rule’ states that any overhang angled greater than 45° from vertical typically requires support structures.”
“Using the 45° rule minimizes the need for support ...” (guidance on when supports are required).
“Support structures leave slight marks where they touch the part; support removal and post‑processing are required to restore surface finish.”
